newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian unions urge C$400 mln govt rescue.
newsitem.headline: Canadian unions urge C$400 mln govt rescue.

text.p: The two biggest unions at Canadian Airlines Corp stood firm against the carrier's restructuring plan on Monday and proposed instead a rescue package under which the federal government would invest C$400 million in the airline over four years.

After a meeting with Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson, leaders of the Canadian Auto Workers union and the Canadian Union of Public Employees repeated that they would not agree to the plan proposed by Canadian, which called for wage cuts.
Four other unions have agreed to support the plan.
CUPE and CAW contend that employees have already sacrificed enough to ensure the airline's survival in the form of previous cutbacks and productivity improvements.

They want the government to re-regulate the airline industry -- something Ottawa has refused to consider. They proposed a plan Monday calling for governments to inject C$100 million a year for the next four years and for Ottawa to take an unspecified equity stake in Canadian.
Officials including Canadian President Kevin Benson and Anderson have said the company-proposed restructuring plan will not fly without the support of all the unions.
CAW president Buzz Hargrove said he would ask British Columbia to provide C$10 million to C$15 million a year of the total and Alberta for a contribution about half the size of British Columbia's.
Hargrove was to meet British Columbia Premier Glen Clark later Monday.

The unions' stance was in contrast to hope expressed earlier in the day by the unions representing Canadian's machinists and pilots. Their officials even held out hope for a deal to be reached Monday but chances for a deal appeared slim as the day progressed.

Anderson was not prepared to make any commitments, CUPE president Judy Darcy said after presenting the proposal to him. Anderson himself said he was a "little disappointed" in the talks compared to the earlier meeting with the unions that have agreed to the restructuring.

He said the government did not have C$400 million to inject in the absence of an agreement by all unions on the restructuring. He refused to specify what sort of financial aid, if any, the government would consider if there was agreement.
Darcy also called for pressure to be applied on Canadians' banks to make greater concessions to keep Canadian aloft. Royal Bank of Canada is one of Canadian's biggest creditors.
Hargrove said re-regulation was essential to ensure the airline does not run into problems again due to cutthroat competition.
"We have given and given and given," said Hargrove. "They can't ask our membership to give any more." CAW and CUPE members are the lowest paid workers at Canadian, he said.
